Twenty-eight comments

Captain Campbell

In Tokyo, there are a couple of fiddlers who really love Cape Breton music and are popularizing several strathspeys in the session. This is one of them.

I feel this tune is melodious enough to mix with Irish tunes while I like playing “A.A. Cameron’s” and modern Scottish reel “Islay Rant” after it. Is there any good Irish reel to follow this one? I’ve just found “Lilting Banshee (Ballinasloe Fair)” is nice, but it’s a jig.

↳ Posted by slainte on March 31st, 2003.

Captain Campbell

Thanks sainte, I like this tune a lot.

↳ Posted by gian marco on April 1st, 2003.

Donegal highland

This is a version of a very well-known highland that’s a standard in Donegal so no problem mixing it with Irish music. This is the version we play locally

The “less than” sign

It looks like if you use the “less than” sign in the comments section then it deletes everything following. I wonder if that’s because the comments may be converted to html or java code at some stage, and the “less than” sign (and the “greater than” sign for that matter) is used functionally in html and java. Perhaps Jeremy could confirm or otherwise.

↳ Posted by fidicen on April 2nd, 2003.

↳ Posted by violinjenn on July 25th, 2020.

Re: Captain Campbell

What you have there, violinjenn, is what I call Captain Campbell’s March (as opposed to Captain Campbell). It’s what pipers would call a 2/4 and it’s not a strathspey (or highland, for that matter).

The first three parts of this tune first appeared in print in [William] Ross’s Collection of Pipe Music in 1869. At a later date (sometime after 1876) David Glen added two more parts, the first of which has become the fourth part of this setting.

Here’s a recently recorded socially distanced take after we picked the tune up from Rua MacMillan:
http://www.riddellfiddles.co.uk/index.php/aiovg_videos/captain-campbells-march-a-foray-into-video-editing/
You’ll also find it in The Glengarry Collection Volume 2 [Mel Bay] - the fiddle music of Aonghas Grant. Since Rua was a student of Aonghas’ maybe that’s where Rua learned the tune.

Campbell is a fairly common name, especially in the Highlands of Scotland and it’s not unusual for there to be more than one Captain Campbell.
